title: Hot Work — Cutting, Grinding, Welding and Soldering on Site
verdict:
No — close, but I will not sign it, and the reason is asbestos.

WHAT I CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED. The shape is right: twelve keys, eleven steps, six keys per step, no extras. Controls run highest-first in every step. No residual exceeds its initial. No admin/PPE-only step claims low. The levelling is genuinely good — I went through all 95 controls looking for the trap and did not find it. The harness is ppe, the secondary-guarding device on the boom is engineering, the gas test is administrative, reading the asbestos register is administrative, the release-to-manual and the actuator lock-off are isolate, the prohibition on hot-cutting a fuel line is administrative. Nothing is dressed up.

On the law I pulled the current consolidations and read the words. WHS Regulation 2011 (Qld), current as at 29 March 2026: s 51(2) reads "(a) the atmosphere does not have a safe oxygen level; or (b) the concentration of oxygen in the atmosphere increases the fire risk; or (c) the concentration of flammable gas, vapour, mist, or fumes exceeds 5% of the LEL" — all three paraphrases in references[3] are right, and Schedule 19 does define safe oxygen level as "a minimum oxygen content in air of 19.5% by volume under normal atmospheric pressure and a maximum oxygen content of air of 23.5% by volume", so the 19.5–23.5 acceptance criteria on the permit come from where the document says they come from. s 52(2) reads "This section does not apply if the ignition source is part of a deliberate process or activity at the workplace" — references[4] telling the reader "s 52 does not reach hot work. Cite s 51" is correct and the old mis-citation is gone. s 291(a), (d), (j), (k), (l), (o) are quoted verbatim. s 425(6) is right. s 529B(1)(b) lists exactly the five measures the SWMS names. Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 (Qld) s 49 and s 53(2) are correct word for word, including the occupier, the approved form, the 24 hours and the 30 penalty units — that finding is properly answered, not gestured at. Fire Services Act 1990 (Qld) s 146N(1) and the example "establishing requirements for persons working near the system to isolate the system while using tools that may cause an unwanted alarm" are verbatim. The 2013 Electrical Safety Regulation appears once, named beside its 2026 replacement, which is allowed. And the two things nobody could verify — the AS 1674.1 edition and the QFD monitoring provider — have been demoted to house rules and to one dated, flagged line, which is the honest way to handle them.

All nine of the previous findings are genuinely closed. The gaseous suppression work is thorough — activity, whenRequired, planning, the walk, the isolate, the shielding step, restoration, permits, training, prompts and emergency all carry it, and the restoration sequence at steps[9].controls[6] and [7] (alarm-test with the actuator still off, refit last) is exactly right. The pump, the oxygen depletion and the EWP crush are all properly built in.

WHY IT STILL FAILS. steps[5].hazards[5] says "Asbestos gasket or lagging on old pipework". Twelve controls follow it and not one of them is about asbestos. The only asbestos control in the whole document is at steps[0].controls[3] and it stops at identification: get the register, and if there is no register and the building is pre-2004, do not cut. It never says what happens when the register says yes, or when you lift a flange and find rope gasket you were not expecting. There is no stop-work rule, no prohibition on putting a grinder or a flame on it, no handoff, and no asbestos training entry — even though hrcw[1] ticks s 291(d) "involves, or is likely to involve, the disturbance of asbestos" as in scope for this statement, and s 445 requires that training. The document does this correctly for confined space: "that work is outside this SWMS and needs its own". Asbestos gets nothing. A technician reads a hazard row with twelve controls beside it and believes it is handled.

Three more the correction did not reach. The multi-gas detector is now the spine of the oxygen controls, but steps[0].controls[4] only puts it on the truck if the site stores flammables — so on a comms room job with no stored fuel it stays in the yard, and steps[7].controls[11] then demands it. steps[9].controls[5] lifts the ASE isolate and closes the reference, and steps[9].controls[6] then alarm-tests a device: that is the brigade turnout the step names as hazards[8], done in the order the document prescribes. And drilling into a plant room wall for a bracket — which this statement puts in scope at steps[6] — has no locate-before-you-drill control anywhere, while steps[1].hazards[3] names "gas lines" behind the wall and hrcw ticks s 291(k).

One note that is not a finding: whenRequired now counts the crew (two, three with a basket, four in a public area) but does not count the traffic spotter steps[4].controls[7] requires in a warehouse. The "if the numbers do not add up" sentence catches it, so I am leaving it alone — but it would read better with the forklift case named.

Fix the asbestos hole, get the detector onto the truck, swap steps[9].controls[5] and [6], and put a control under the drill, and I would sign it.

blocking.field: steps[5].hazards[5] "Asbestos gasket or lagging on old pipework" — against all twelve of steps[5].controls; also steps[0].hazards[2], steps[0].controls[3], hrcw[1], training (no entry), emergency (no entry)
blocking.problem: The document names asbestos twice as a hazard and never controls its disturbance. steps[5].hazards[5] is "Asbestos gasket or lagging on old pipework" and not one of the twelve controls in that step mentions asbestos. The only asbestos control in the whole statement is steps[0].controls[3], and it is an identification gate only: get the register, and "No register and a pre-2004 building means no cutting into building fabric until it has been identified." It is silent on the branch that actually happens — the register says there IS lagging or a rope gasket on that line, or the technician lifts a flange mid-job and finds suspect material. There is no stop-work-on-discovery rule, no prohibition on grinding, cutting, wire-brushing or heating ACM, no handoff to the asbestos statement this company already ships, no mention of licensed removal, and no asbestos entry in training at all — while hrcw[1] ticks WHS Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 291(d) "involves, or is likely to involve, the disturbance of asbestos" as in scope, and s 445 requires training in the identification and safe handling of asbestos and ACM for workers who may do this work. Heat makes it worse in a way the document never says: a bonded gasket that has been under a torch is no longer non-friable. The statement handles the identical situation correctly for confined space ("that work is outside this SWMS and needs its own") and for gaseous suppression, so a crew reading a hazard row with twelve controls beside it will reasonably believe asbestos is one of the things those controls cover.
blocking.fix: Add an administrative control to steps[5], placed with the other stop rules immediately before the existing controls[8] ("Never hot-cut a line that has held anything but water or air"): "Look at what is on the old line before the blade or the flame goes near it. Rope gasket, millboard, or lagging on pre-2004 pipework is asbestos until a sample says otherwise. You do not grind it, cut it, wire-brush it or heat it — heat turns a bonded gasket friable. Stop, tape it off, ring the office. Service work on non-friable ACM fixed before 31 December 2003 is only allowed under the rest of chapter 8 (WHS Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 419(3)(c)); a power tool does not go on ACM unless its use is controlled — enclosed, or designed to capture or suppress the dust (s 446(3) and (4)); removal is a licensed asbestos removalist's job (s 458), except 10 m2 or less of non-friable material, which still needs a competent person trained under s 445 (s 458(2)(a) and (3)). That work is outside this SWMS and goes onto the asbestos statement." Add to whenRequired the same hard exclusion the document already gives confined space. Add a training entry: "Asbestos awareness — identification and safe handling of asbestos and ACM and the control measures for it, WHS Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 445, for anyone who may disturb ACM on old pipework or building fabric." Add to emergency: "SUSPECT ASBESTOS DISTURBED: stop, everybody out, do not sweep it and do not blow it down with compressed air (s 446(1)), tape the room off, ring the office and the occupier, and nobody goes back in until it has been assessed." Add to references: s 419 (work involving asbestos — prohibitions and exceptions), s 445 (duty to train workers about asbestos), s 446 (duty to limit use of equipment), s 458 (duty to ensure asbestos removalist is licensed). Add to siteSpecificPrompts: "What are the flange gaskets and the pipe lagging on the line you are cutting, and who confirmed it?"

blocking.field: steps[0].controls[4], last sentence — against steps[7].controls[11], steps[5].controls[5] and siteSpecificPrompts[16]
blocking.problem: The multi-gas detector is now the spine of the oxygen-depletion controls, and the only thing that puts it on the truck is steps[0].controls[4]: "...whether the site stores LPG, fuel, solvents, chlorinated degreasers or combustible dust anywhere near the work. If the answer to that last one is yes or unknown, the multi-gas detector comes with you." That trigger is stored flammables only. But the room that kills you by oxygen displacement is the small unventilated plant room or comms room where argon or CO2 shielding gas pools at the floor — and such a room typically stores nothing. steps[7].controls[11] then says "In any small or unventilated plant room it runs whether or not that test applied" and training[6] says "The instrument that comes on a hot work job is a multi-gas detector." So the document requires an instrument on site that its own planning step did not require anybody to bring. siteSpecificPrompts[16] repeats the same narrow trigger. A crew that answers "no stored flammables" the day before arrives without the detector, and then either does not strike the arc or — far more likely at 3pm in a comms room — strikes it anyway. The oxygen control added in the last round does not reach the yard.
blocking.fix: Rewrite the last sentence of steps[0].controls[4] so the detector comes on any of three triggers, not one: "The multi-gas detector comes with you if any of these is yes or unknown — the site stores LPG, fuel, solvents, degreasers or combustible dust anywhere near the work; the pipe or vessel you are cutting into may hold vapour; or any part of the work is arc welding, brazing or gas cutting in a plant room, comms room, riser cupboard or any room you cannot stand in and prove is ventilated. If it is not on the truck, the arc does not get struck in that room." Amend siteSpecificPrompts[16] to ask all three. Say plainly somewhere in whenRequired that the multi-gas detector is standard kit on a hot work job, matching what training[6] already claims.

blocking.field: steps[9].controls[5] and steps[9].controls[6], in that order — against steps[9].hazards[8]
blocking.problem: controls[5] says "Ring the monitoring contractor to lift the ASE isolate, confirm the signal path is back, and close out the isolation reference." controls[6] then says "Prove the work. Alarm-test a device on the affected zone and confirm the correct zone and point reports at the FIP." Done in that order, the alarm test signals through a live ASE to a monitoring centre that is not expecting it, and the brigade turns out — which is exactly steps[9].hazards[8], "Unwanted alarm and brigade turnout when the system is restored". The document names the hazard and then instructs the thing that causes it. It matters beyond the embarrassment: under Fire Services Act 1990 (Qld) s 146N(1) the occupier must maintain the monitored system so an unacceptable number of unwanted alarms are not signalled, and s 146N(2) makes the number unacceptable once it is "more than 4" since the end of the last financial year and more than the average the commissioner publishes. A false turnout the crew caused goes on the client's count. There is also nothing telling the technician how the signal path is actually proved — "confirm the signal path is back" over the phone is not a test.
blocking.fix: Swap the two controls and add the missing step. New order: alarm-test the device on the affected zone with the ASE STILL ISOLATED and confirm the correct zone and point at the FIP (keeping the existing gaseous rule — release on manual-only, actuator still off the cylinder). Then, last: "Ring the monitoring provider, tell them a test signal is coming, and stay on the line. Lift the ASE isolate, put up one test signal, and do not hang up until they have told you they received it and logged it as a test. Then close out the isolation reference. An alarm signal that reaches monitoring with nobody expecting it is an unwanted alarm and a brigade turnout, and unwanted alarms count against the occupier under Fire Services Act 1990 (Qld) s 146N — more than 4 since the end of the last financial year and more than the published average and they are in breach." Keep the ASE restoration inside the witnessed countersign at controls[8].

blocking.field: steps[6] "Cutting and grinding" — hazards (none for this) and controls (none for this); also steps[1].hazards[3] / steps[1].controls[2], hrcw, siteSpecificPrompts[11]
blocking.problem: This statement puts drilling into masonry and concrete for brackets squarely in scope (steps[6].hazards[3], controls[3], controls[7]) and never names what is buried in the wall or slab. There is no hazard entry and no control anywhere for striking a live cable, a conduit, a gas pipe or a hydraulic line while drilling or coring. The document comes close twice and stops: steps[1].hazards[3] names "Voids, cable tray, gas lines and stock on the far side of the wall you are cutting near", and the only control for it is steps[1].controls[2], "physically look at the other side of every wall" — which tells you nothing about what is inside a masonry wall or a slab, and nothing at all where the far side is a locked tenancy the same control elsewhere acknowledges you cannot get into. siteSpecificPrompts[11] asks the question and no control answers it. The RCD at steps[6].controls[4] does not help here: it monitors the tool's own supply, not fault current arriving through the bit from a cable you have just drilled into. hrcw ticks s 291(k) "is carried out on or near energised electrical installations or services" as applying on nearly every plant room job, so the statement promises to handle this and then does not, and it omits s 291(i) "is carried out on or near pressurised gas distribution mains or piping" altogether while naming gas lines behind the wall as a hazard.
blocking.fix: Add to steps[6].hazards: "Drilling or coring into a wall, slab or soffit and hitting what is buried in it — live cable, conduit, gas pipe, hydraulic or refrigerant line. There is no warning, and the RCD on your own lead does not protect you from current arriving through the bit." Add an administrative control at the head of the admin block in steps[6] (before the existing controls[5]): "Before you drill or core, get the as-installed services drawings, scan the fixing zone with a cable and service locator, and mark what you find on the wall. Treat every wall and slab as live until you have. Where a service is confirmed in the fixing zone, move the bracket, or have that circuit or line isolated under the electrical isolation permit before the bit goes in — licensed electrical worker, locked and tagged. Do not core a post-tensioned slab without the structural engineer's sign-off." Add s 291(i) to hrcw, quoted as "is carried out on or near pressurised gas distribution mains or piping", and name it in the whenRequired paragraph that tells the crew which classifications to tick — (i) applies wherever the work is near the building's gas reticulation.

blocking.field: steps[4].hazards[4] "Poor footing on a wet, oily or cluttered plant room floor" — against all nine of steps[4].controls; and steps[6].controls[2]
blocking.problem: The hazard is named and no control in the step, or anywhere else, addresses it. The closest is steps[4].controls[4], and that is about the machine, not the person: "the floor checked for penetrations, pits and load rating before the machine goes on it." Meanwhile the document actively creates the condition it named — steps[6].controls[2] says "Where you are grinding on a concrete floor, wet the floor down first" — and the only housekeeping in the statement is at steps[10].controls[2], after the work is finished: "Clean the floor, clear the drip trays." So for the whole job the floor is wet, oily, strewn with swarf and crossed by welding leads, gas hoses and extension leads, with somebody walking backwards under a lit torch, and nothing says anything about it.
blocking.fix: Add an administrative control to steps[4], after controls[7]: "Housekeeping before the work position goes in and all the way through it. Welding leads, gas hoses and extension leads run overhead or hard against the wall, never across the walking route between the work, the extinguishers and the door. Standing water, oil and spills dealt with before you set up, not at the end. Offcuts, discs and swarf go into the quench bucket as they are made. Where the floor has been wet down for sparks under steps[6], barricade the wet area and keep the walking route and the route to the extinguishers dry."

blocking.field: steps[7].controls[1], second sentence: "Keep the plant room door closed or screened"
blocking.problem: This is the arc-flash control, and in most plant rooms the door is the ventilation. The rest of this step now turns on oxygen displacement — hazards[6] warns that argon and CO2 pool at low level and "you get no warning at all", controls[2] requires forced ventilation to stop the shielding gas displacing the air you are breathing, and controls[11] has the detector running with a 19.5–23.5% stop trigger. Telling a welder to shut the door of a small plant room is the single most direct way to create the atmosphere the step is written to prevent, and it sits four controls above the ventilation rule so it is read first. "Closed or screened" leaves the choice to a technician who is being told to stop the arc getting out. It also cuts across steps[5].controls[2], which requires the plant room ventilated or the roller door open before a diesel pump can run.
blocking.fix: Rewrite the sentence: "Screen the doorway — do not shut it. In most plant rooms that door is the ventilation, and shutting it with argon, CO2, purge gas or a fuel gas in the room is how the oxygen goes. If the only way to keep the arc off people outside is to shut the door, then mechanical extraction runs the whole time or the work does not proceed. The door also stays open or screened wherever a diesel pump can start."

blocking.field: steps[2].controls[5] "Cap only the detectors in the room you are working in" — and the matching restoration proof at steps[9].controls[0]
blocking.problem: The isolation control assumes point detectors on a ceiling, and the restoration proof assumes a cap count: "write the number of caps on the job card, and photograph each cap as it goes on. You will count them back against those photos", then steps[9].controls[0] "Count the detector caps back in against the number on the job card." That does not fit the rooms this correction has just written the statement around. permits[3] names data centres, cold stores, hospitals and shopping centres, and steps[2].controls[0] is about comms rooms with gaseous suppression — which are precisely the rooms protected by aspirating detection that samples through a pipe and cannot be capped, by in-duct detectors sitting in the air handling return, and by beam detectors that cannot be covered. A technician who caps the two point detectors he can see and grinds has still put his smoke down a VESDA sampling pipe. With the actuator locked off nobody dies, but he gets an unwanted alarm, a brigade turnout, and on most sites a fire trip that shuts down the air handling — which removes the ventilation that steps[7].controls[2] and controls[11] depend on to keep the oxygen up. And because there is no cap to count, the cap-count-back proof at steps[9].controls[0] passes clean with a panel isolate still on.
blocking.fix: Add to steps[2].controls[5]: "Not every room is protected by point detectors. Aspirating detection (VESDA and the like) samples through a pipe and cannot be capped, in-duct detectors sit in the air handling return and will see your smoke from a room away, and beam detectors cannot be covered. Where the room has any of those, isolate them at the panel instead, write down exactly what you isolated — not a cap count — and put it on the impairment permit as its own line. Ask the building's responsible person what happens on a fire trip: on most sites it shuts the air handling down, and that is the ventilation this statement relies on." Amend steps[9].controls[0] to read: "Count the caps back against the job card and the photos, AND clear every panel isolate you wrote on the permit, item by item. A cap count does not prove an aspirating or duct detector is back on."

blocking.problem: permits[2] and steps[2].controls[3] both make booking the ASE isolate a precondition — "Book the ASE isolate with the QFD-contracted alarm monitoring provider before you isolate" — and references[29] now deliberately withholds the provider and the number, correctly, because they could not be verified: "Last checked: not confirmed... not to be quoted to a site until somebody opens qfd.qld.gov.au, confirms them and writes the details and the date they checked here." That is the honest call and I would not undo it. But it leaves a technician standing at a FIP with a mandatory step and no way to complete it, and the failure mode when a crew cannot complete a mandatory step at 3pm is that they isolate without booking and turn the brigade out — the exact outcome the control exists to prevent. The document knows the name of the volatile fact but not the route to it, and the route is on site: the monitoring provider is identified on the ASE and the monitoring equipment at the FIP, and the occupier holds the account and the account number.
blocking.fix: Add the on-the-day route to permits[2] and steps[2].controls[3]: "Who to ring is on the building, not in this document. The monitoring provider is identified on the ASE and the monitoring equipment at the FIP — photograph the label at steps[1] — and the occupier holds the monitoring account and account number. Get both from the building's responsible person before you touch anything. Ring them, book the isolate, write the reference they give you on the permit." Keep references[29] as the single dated line for the QFD-contracted provider and the duration threshold above which Queensland Fire Department approval is needed, and confirm and date it before this SWMS is issued.
